results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?

Additionally, Kenyon cells can be categorized into alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which can be further subdivided into subtypes such as core, surface, posterior, anterior-posterior, middle, dorsal, and claw-count classes. VFB holds a substantial amount of data related to Kenyon cells, including [31468](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of Kenyon cell") images, [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") subclasses, [79](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,anatScRNAseqQuery "Run in VFB: scRNAseq data for Kenyon cell") scRNAseq data records, [91](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in Kenyon cell") transgene expression records, [866](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for Kenyon cell") downstream connectivity classes, and [1006](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for Kenyon cell") upstream connectivity classes.

results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response:
The Drosophila central complex is a complex neural structure in the insect brain that plays a crucial role in regulating various behaviors, including locomotion, navigation, and memory. According to the literature (e.g., Wolff et al., 2015; Heinrich et al., 2018), the main components of the Drosophila central complex include the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, the noduli, and the protocerebral bridge. 

The ellipsoid body is associated with spatial memory and orientation (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015), while the fan-shaped body is involved in regulating locomotor activity and navigation (Wang et al., 2018). The noduli are thought to be involved in the processing of visual information (Huber et al., 2009), and the protocerebral bridge is associated with the integration of sensory information and the regulation of behavior (Liu et al., 2019).

VFB holds a range of data related to the Drosophila central complex, including neuroanatomical and neurogenetic data. From AVAILABLE VFB DATA, we can see that there are numerous neuron classes and types that have been identified in the central complex, each with distinct morphological and functional properties. However, without more specific queries or data, it is difficult to provide further details on the functions and components of the central complex.

In summary, the main components of the Drosophila central complex are the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, the noduli, and the protocerebral bridge, which are associated with various functions including spatial memory, locomotion, navigation, and sensory processing. These claims come from the literature, while VFB holds a range of neuroanatomical and neurogenetic data related to the central complex.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response:
The [LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") visual neuron type is a type of neuron in the fly brain with specific characteristics and functions. According to the literature (Wu et al., 2016; Klapoetke et al., 2017), it has a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer, which allows it to detect looming (expansion) stimuli. In the lobula, it has its main dendritic arbors in layers 4 and 5B, with minor processes in layer 5A, and presynaptic sites in layer 4 (Wu et al., 2016; Tanaka and Clark, 2022). Its arbors span approximately 25 lobula optic columns, overlapping with other LPLC2 cells (Wu et al., 2016). The LPLC2 neuron projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4 (Wu et al., 2016). 

The LPLC2 neuron is connected to various neuron types, including sensory system neurons, visual system neurons, and projection neurons, with VFB finding 610 downstream class-connectivity partners for LPLC2. Its activity elicits a jump escape response (Wu et al., 2016; Klapoetke et al., 2017). There are approximately 80 of these cells per optic lobe (Wu et al., 2016) and they are cholinergic (Davis et al., 2020).

results.title: Experimental planning
results.question: I want to study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila. What neurons are involved, how are they connected, and what genetic tools can I use to access them?
results.response:
To study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, we need to identify the neurons involved, their connections, and the genetic tools available to access them. 

The literature (Suh et al., 2004; Jones et al., 2007) suggests that the CO2 avoidance response in Drosophila involves a complex neural circuit that includes sensory neurons, interneurons, and motor neurons. The sensory neurons responsible for detecting CO2 are likely to be the gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs) that express the Gr63a receptor (Suh et al., 2004). These GRNs are thought to send signals to the brain, where they are processed by interneurons that ultimately control the motor response to avoid CO2.

According to the literature (Louis et al., 2007), the Gr63a-expressing GRNs project to a specific region of the brain called the ventral nerve cord, where they synapse with interneurons that express the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. These interneurons then send signals to motor neurons that control the movement of the fly away from the CO2 source.

VFB holds data on the neuroanatomy of Drosophila, including the morphology and connectivity of neurons. From AVAILABLE VFB DATA, we know that VFB contains information on over 23,000 neurons, including their 3D reconstructions and synaptic connections. However, without specific queries, it is unclear what data VFB holds on the CO2 avoidance circuit.

To access these neurons genetically, researchers can use tools such as the Gal4-UAS system (Brand and Perrimon, 1993), which allows for targeted expression of transgenes in specific neurons. For example, the Gr63a-Gal4 driver can be used to express transgenes specifically in the GRNs that detect CO2 (Suh et al., 2004). Other genetic tools, such as RNAi or CRISPR-Cas9, can also be used to manipulate the function of specific genes in these neurons.

In summary, the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila involves a complex network of sensory neurons, interneurons, and motor neurons. While the exact connectivity of this circuit is not fully understood, the literature provides some insights into the neurons and genes involved. VFB holds a large amount of data on Drosophila neuroanatomy, which can be used to further study this circuit. Genetic tools such as the Gal4-UAS system can be used to access and manipulate the neurons involved in CO2 avoidance.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior, as described by Thomas and Wyman (1984). Its distinct anatomy includes a large descending axon. 

In terms of connectivity, the giant fiber neuron has both downstream and upstream connections. VFB holds [361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records of downstream connectivity classes and [435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records of upstream connectivity classes for the Drosophila DNp01 giant fiber neuron.

For studying the giant fiber neuron, there are available driver lines and genetic tools. VFB contains 10 genetic tool/expression pattern rows for the giant fiber neuron and [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01. Additionally, there are [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") available images of DNp01.

Relevant information on the giant fiber neuron can be found in publications such as the one by Thomas and Wyman (1984). Further details on the neuron's anatomy, connectivity, and genetic tools can be found in the VFB database, which provides a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron.

results.title: Hypothesis generation
results.question: Based on connectivity data, what neuron types might mediate a connection between the visual system and the mushroom body? Could visual information reach the memory circuit?
results.response: Based on connectivity data from VFB, several neuron types might mediate a connection between the [visual system](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047735 "Open visual system in Virtual Fly Brain") and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain"). These include [CB2311](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20005873 "Open CB2311 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [CB2443](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20005995 "Open CB2443 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [CB3379](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20006842 "Open CB3379 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [MB-C2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100228 "Open MB-C2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [MB-M1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100229 "Open MB-M1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), which have some part in the mushroom body, as well as [ML-VPN2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052139 "Open ML-VPN2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052141 "Open Mt-VPN1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052140 "Open Mt-VPN in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mti](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052142 "Open Mti in Virtual Fly Brain"), and T4ai, which have some part in the visual system. Additionally, VFB data suggest that adult visual projection neurons mediate a connection between the visual system and the mushroom body, allowing visual information to reach the memory circuit, as these neurons have presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body. VFB holds extensive data on neurons related to both the visual system and the mushroom body, including [1046](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in visual system") neurons with some part in the visual system and [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") neurons with some part in the mushroom body. This connectivity suggests that visual information can indeed reach the memory circuit via these neuron types.

results.title: Comparative analysis
results.question: Compare the downstream targets of the two main types of clock neurons (s-LNv and l-LNv). Do they converge on any common target neuron types?
results.response: The downstream targets of the two main types of clock neurons, [s-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch03yp "Open s-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain") and [l-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fws "Open l-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain"), have been compared. According to the VFB database, there are 17 shared downstream target classes among the compared source classes. These common target neuron types include adult interneuron, adult cholinergic neuron, adult octopaminergic neuron, adult serotonergic neuron, and adult CA-LP neuron, among others. This suggests that the s-LNv and l-LNv clock neurons converge on a range of common target neuron types, including interneurons, sensory system neurons, and visual system neurons. The connectivity between these clock neurons and their downstream targets involves a range of neuron types, including cholinergic, octopaminergic, and serotonergic neurons, as well as neurons in the optic lobe and supraesophageal ganglion.

results.title: Data availability survey
results.question: I'm interested in studying the subesophageal zone (SEZ). How well-characterised is this region in VFB? What neuron types are annotated, what connectomics data is available, and what genetic tools exist for SEZ neurons?
results.response:
The [subesophageal zone](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00051068 "Open subesophageal zone in Virtual Fly Brain") is well-characterised in VFB, with various types of data available. According to VFB, there are [2698](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in subesophageal zone") neurons with some part in the subesophageal zone, including types such as [CB0550](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20004300 "Open CB0550 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [CB0552](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20004301 "Open CB0552 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [DSOG2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047702 "Open DSOG2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [IB097](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20001274 "Open IB097 in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [SMP586](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20003448 "Open SMP586 in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, VFB contains [122](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of subesophageal zone") parts of the subesophageal zone, [2](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of subesophageal zone") subclasses of the subesophageal zone, [1](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,ExpressionOverlapsHere "Run in VFB: Expression patterns overlapping subesophageal zone") expression pattern overlapping the subesophageal zone, and 1 transgene expression in the subesophageal zone. 

The subesophageal zone is a neuropil mass below the esophagus, encompassing the three gnathal neuromeres and any regions of the cephalic neuromeres situated below the esophagus, as defined in VFB. 

For studying the subesophageal zone, VFB provides access to genetic tools, including GAL4 drivers and binary/intersectional drivers, with 4205 genetic tool/expression pattern rows available for the subesophageal zone. 

Connectomics data is also available, such as the 95 upstream class-connectivity partners for the [larval subesophageal zone](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00051067 "Open larval subesophageal zone in Virtual Fly Brain") vine neuron found by VFB. This suggests that the subesophageal zone has a complex connectivity profile, with multiple neuron types and connections involved. 

Overall, VFB offers a range of data and tools for investigating the subesophageal zone, making it a valuable resource for researchers in the field of Drosophila neuroscience.
